title: What are the CQRS trade-offs — benefits (independent scaling of reads/writes, optimized read models, simpler write logic focused on invariants, easier to add new query shapes without touching the domain) vs costs (eventual consistency between write and read models, data duplication, more code/infrastructure, projection rebuild complexity) — and when should you NOT use CQRS (simple CRUD apps, low traffic, when strong consistency between write and read is required on every request, when the team doesn't need independent read/write scaling)?
shortTitle: What are the CQRS trade-offs and when should you NOT use CQRS

s1_definition.profdef: CQRS trades simplicity for separation. The benefits are independent scaling of the read and write sides, read models optimized for specific query shapes, write logic kept simple and focused on invariants, and the freedom to add new query shapes without touching the domain. The costs are eventual consistency between the write and read models, data duplication, more code and infrastructure, and the operational complexity of rebuilding projections. You should not use it for simple CRUD, low traffic, when every request needs strong write-then-read consistency, or when you do not need to scale reads and writes separately.
s1_definition.analogy: Running two separate counters at National Bank of India is powerful when the branch is huge and busy, but for a tiny village branch with five customers a day it is wasteful. You now need two sets of records that must be kept in sync, and for a brief moment after a transfer the display board might still show the old balance even though the ledger already changed. If the branch is small, one combined counter is simpler and always perfectly up to date.
s1_definition.oneliner: CQRS buys independent scaling and fast tailored reads at the price of eventual consistency, duplicated data, and more moving parts, so skip it for simple, low-traffic, strongly-consistent CRUD.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** CQRS trades simplicity for separation. The benefits are independent scaling of the read and write sides, read models optimized for specific query shapes, write logic kept simple and focused on invariants, and the freedom to add new query shapes without touching the domain. The costs are eventual consistency between the write and read models, data duplication, more code and infrastructure, and the operational complexity of rebuilding projections. You should not use it for simple CRUD, low traffic, when every request needs strong write-then-read consistency, or when you do not need to scale reads and writes separately.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Running two separate counters at National Bank of India is powerful when the branch is huge and busy, but for a tiny village branch with five customers a day it is wasteful. You now need two sets of records that must be kept in sync, and for a brief moment after a transfer the display board might still show the old balance even though the ledger already changed. If the branch is small, one combined counter is simpler and always perfectly up to date.

**One line to remember:** CQRS buys independent scaling and fast tailored reads at the price of eventual consistency, duplicated data, and more moving parts, so skip it for simple, low-traffic, strongly-consistent CRUD.

sections.s2_technical:
Start with the benefits because they are the reason anyone adopts CQRS. Independent scaling means that because reads vastly outnumber writes in most banking systems, you can run many read-side instances off cheap denormalized stores while keeping a small, carefully controlled write side. Optimized read models mean each screen is backed by a projection shaped exactly for it, so a dashboard query is one indexed read instead of a multi-table join. Simpler write logic means the aggregate only cares about protecting invariants, with no reporting or query concerns cluttering the money-moving code. And adding a new query shape is cheap: you build a new projection by consuming existing events, with zero changes to the domain model.

Now the costs, which are the heart of a senior answer. Eventual consistency is the big one. Because the read model is updated after the write commits, there is a window where a client who just wrote and immediately reads may see stale data. For example right after a transfer the balance view might momentarily show the old figure. You must design the UI and APIs to tolerate this, for instance by returning the command result directly or by showing a pending state. Data duplication is inherent: the same information lives in the normalized write model and in one or more denormalized read models, which costs storage and introduces the possibility of drift if projections have bugs. More code and infrastructure is a real tax: commands, handlers, events, projections, and two sets of repositories are more to build, test, and operate than a single CRUD model. Projection rebuild complexity means that when a projection schema changes or a bug corrupts it, you need a disciplined way to rebuild it from the source of truth, which requires either replaying events or re-reading the write model, plus careful handling of live traffic during the rebuild.

When should you deliberately not use CQRS? For simple CRUD applications where reads and writes use the same shape, the separation adds cost with no benefit. For low-traffic systems the scaling argument disappears, so the extra complexity is pure overhead. When strong consistency between write and read is required on every single request, such as a screen that must always show the exact committed balance with zero staleness tolerance, eventual consistency is a liability and a single consistent model is safer. And when the team genuinely does not need to scale reads and writes independently, you are paying for a capability you will never use.

A senior nuance is that CQRS is not all-or-nothing and not the same as event sourcing. You can apply it to only the few aggregates that need it while the rest of the system stays plain CRUD. The lightest form shares one database with two models and synchronous projection, which removes the eventual-consistency cost at the price of giving up independent scaling. Choosing where on that spectrum to sit is the actual engineering decision, and the mistake juniors make is adopting full event-sourced CQRS everywhere by default.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India's reference-data service for branch addresses is a tiny CRUD table edited a few times a month, yet a well-meaning architect proposed full CQRS for it. This is exactly a case where CQRS should not be used, because there is no read-write skew, no scaling need, and the added code would be pure overhead.

Problem 2 — The high-traffic account-statement feature, by contrast, serves millions of reads against the same tables that process transfers, and reporting load was slowing down money movement. This is exactly where CQRS pays off, because a denormalized read model lets reads scale independently and keeps the write path clean.

Problem 3 — After a transfer, a naive screen read the read model immediately and briefly showed the old balance, confusing customers. This illustrates the eventual-consistency cost, which we must handle by returning the committed result from the command or showing a pending indicator.

Our mini-project builds a small decision helper and demonstrates both the benefit and the cost. The code defines a `CqrsSuitabilityScorer` that scores a workload against the decision criteria and recommends CQRS or plain CRUD, an `Account` write model, a read `BalanceView`, an eventually-consistent `ProjectionUpdater`, and a demo that shows the stale-read window right after a transfer and then shows the corrected read, plus two suitability evaluations (reference data versus statements).

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: debit 50000 from SAV2001 (Rajesh, 1000000); then score two workloads.

Step 1: The write side loads Rajesh, debits 50000, and saves, so the write model now holds 950000. The data changed only in the write store.

Step 2: A client immediately reads the `BalanceView`, which still holds 1000000 because the projection has not run yet. This is the eventual-consistency cost made visible: a stale read.

Step 3: The `ProjectionUpdater` processes the change and rewrites the `BalanceView` to 950000. Now a read returns the correct figure. The lag between step 1 and step 3 is the consistency window.

Step 4: The suitability scorer evaluates the branch-address workload: low traffic, no scaling need, so it recommends plain CRUD because CQRS overhead is unjustified.

Step 5: The scorer evaluates the account-statement workload: high traffic, read-to-write skew of fifty to one, scaling needed, and no strong read-after-write requirement, so it recommends CQRS because the benefits outweigh the costs.

```
2026-10-24 14:08:40 INFO    WRITE committed: SAV2001 balance now Rs.950000
2026-10-24 14:08:40 WARNING STALE READ: BalanceView still shows Rs.1000000
2026-10-24 14:08:40 INFO    CONSISTENT READ: BalanceView now shows Rs.950000
2026-10-24 14:08:40 INFO    DECISION branch-address → PLAIN CRUD — low traffic / no scaling need; CQRS overhead not justified
2026-10-24 14:08:40 INFO    DECISION account-statement → CQRS — read/write skew 50.0:1, high traffic, independent scaling needed; benefits outweigh costs
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The honest way to talk about CQRS is to lead with the trade-offs rather than treating it as a silver bullet. The benefits are real: the read and write sides scale independently, which matters enormously in banking where reads outnumber writes by a large factor; the read models are optimized for specific query shapes so a dashboard is one indexed read instead of a multi-table join; the write logic stays simple because the aggregate only protects invariants; and I can add a brand-new query shape just by building a new projection without touching the domain at all.

But those benefits come at a price I am always upfront about. The biggest cost is eventual consistency: because the read model is updated after the write commits, there is a window where a client who just wrote and immediately reads can see stale data, and I have to design the UI and APIs to tolerate that, for example by returning the command result directly or showing a pending state. On top of that there is data duplication between the normalized write model and the denormalized read models, more code and infrastructure to build and operate, and the genuine operational complexity of rebuilding a projection when its schema changes or a bug corrupts it.

Because of those costs I am equally clear about when not to use CQRS. For simple CRUD where reads and writes share the same shape, it adds cost with no benefit. For low-traffic systems the scaling argument evaporates, so it is pure overhead. When every request must have strong read-after-write consistency, such as a screen that must always show the exact committed balance, eventual consistency becomes a liability and a single consistent model is safer. And when the team simply does not need to scale reads and writes independently, you are paying for a capability you will never use.

On my platform at National Bank of India I made exactly this distinction. The branch-address reference data is a tiny table edited a few times a month, so I deliberately kept it plain CRUD and pushed back when someone proposed CQRS for it. The account-statement feature, however, served millions of reads against the very tables that process transfers, with a read-to-write skew of about fifty to one and no strong read-after-write requirement, so there CQRS was clearly worth it and we introduced a denormalized read model fed by events. I also stress that CQRS is not all-or-nothing and not the same as event sourcing; I apply it only to the few aggregates that need it and choose the lightest form that still solves the problem.

The one-line summary I give an interviewer is that CQRS buys independent scaling and fast tailored reads at the cost of eventual consistency, duplicated data, and more moving parts, so I apply it only to high-skew, high-traffic aggregates that tolerate staleness, and I keep simple, low-traffic, strongly-consistent workloads as plain CRUD.
